inline.s: Please note that Master Yongming says: if it is

â€œwithout a mind of thought-after-thought continuity, and a will to break off again and again,â€ then rebirth is hard to attain. Therefore, what Master Yongming calls â€œthe ten thoughts at death being accomplishedâ€ means accomplishing the ten thoughts of continual recitation at the moment of death. â€œDedicating to that hourâ€ means dedicating to the moment of death; â€œthought after thought without lapseâ€ means continuing thought after thought without break. Hence, â€œdedicating to that hour, thought after thought without lapseâ€ means dedicating to the moment of death continual thought-after-thought continuity. So then, â€œthere is nothing to fearâ€ (i.e., one is thus able to be assured of rebirth in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss).
On this, Master Daochuo also instructed in the Collected Essays on the Peaceful Grove:
â€œ
For all sentient beings, at the moment of death
, the knife-wind severs the body, the suffering of death presses upon them, and great terror arises. Therefore, meeting a good spiritual friend, they rouse great bravery,
and recite ten thoughts with mind after mind continuing
, and this is a superior root of goodness,
and they attain rebirth
Please note that here Master Daochuo teaches: for all sentient beings, at the moment of death, ten thoughts with mind after mind continuing, and they attain rebirth. That is:
ten thoughts at the moment of death, unbroken thought brings rebirth.

[Knife-wind] When a person is dying, he fully experiences the suffering of death, and the four great elements separate. Among these, the wind that severs the limbs and joints like a knife is called the â€œknife-wind.â€ The Sutra of Right Dharma Mindfulness says: â€œAt the end of life, the knife-winds all stir, and the skin, flesh, sinews, bones, marrow, fat, essence, and blood are all cut and severed.â€ The Sutra of the Five Kings says: â€œWhen about to die, the knife-wind severs the body, and there is no place without pain.â€
Therefore, regarding the meaning of the Eighteenth Vow, Master Daochuo clearly instructs in the Collected Essays on the Peaceful Grove:
â€œIf there are sentient beings who, even having committed evil all their lives, at the moment of death
recite for ten thoughts continually,
calling upon my name,
and are not reborn, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.â€
Here, Master Daochuo has given a precise explanation of the meaning of â€œeven down to ten thoughtsâ€ in the Eighteenth Vow:
at the moment of death, ten thoughts continually, calling upon my name.
Therefore, the â€œeven down to ten thoughtsâ€ of the Eighteenth Vow is the ten thoughts at death, and moreover the ten thoughts that continue without break.
Conclusion Two: From this we know, the â€œeven down to ten thoughtsâ€ of the Eighteenth Vow
is
the ten thoughts at death that continue thought after thought
Regarding
the ten thoughts of continual recitation at death, Master Daochuo, in the Collected Essays on the Peaceful Grove, has another very important instruction, now transcribed and annotated below:

[Question: The Great Sutra of Immeasurable Life says: â€œSentient beings of the ten directions, with utmost sincerity and joyful faith, wishing to be reborn in my land, even down to ten thoughts, and if not reborn, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.â€ Now there are people in the world who, hearing this sage teaching, in this present life pay no attention to it, and intend only at the moment of death to apply their recitation. What about this?]

Question: The Sutra of Immeasurable Life says: â€œSentient beings of the ten directions, with utmost sincerity and joyful faith, wishing to be reborn in my land, even down to ten thoughts, and if not reborn, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.â€ Now there are people who, hearing this sage teaching, behave as if paying no attention, and plan only at the moment of death to accomplish the ten thoughts of continual recitation. Pray tell, what do you think of this plan?
[Answer: This plan is not fitting. Why? The sutra speaks of â€œ
ten thoughts continually

,â€ which seems not difficult. Yet all ordinary beings have minds like wild horses, consciousness more restless than apes, galloping among the six sense-objects â€” when have they ever rested? Each must arouse faith and prepare by restraining his thoughts in advance,
so as to form them into a habit

, and so make his root of goodness firm. As the Buddha told the great king: â€œIf a person accumulates good acts, he will have no evil thought at death; just as a tree that has first leaned over must, when it falls, follow the bent direction.â€ If the knife-wind arrives, and a hundred sufferings join in the body, and the practice was not there beforehand, how could the recollection he wishes to achieve be carried out
(be accomplished)

Answer: This plan is to dig a well when already thirsty. Digging a well when thirsty and preparing the ferry and the bridge in advance are two different matters (this is not fitting). Why? The sutra says â€œten thoughts continually,â€ which seems not difficult (hence many people think they will be able to do it at the moment of death). Yet all ordinary beings have minds like wild horses, consciousness more restless than apes, galloping among the six sense-objects (sight, sound, smell, taste, touch, and mental objects) â€” when have they ever rested? Each must arouse a mind of one-mind faith and prepare by training his thought to be single and his ten thoughts continual, so that it forms into a habit (through constant practice, making the thought single and the ten thoughts continual become an instinct), and only then, at the moment of death, will his root of goodness be firm. As the Buddha told the great king: â€œIf people constantly accumulate good acts, then at death they will have no evil thought; just as when a tree falls over, it must fall toward the direction in which it was already leaning.â€ If the knife-wind of death arrives and a hundred sufferings press and scorch, and beforehand one has not accomplished the ten thoughts of continual recitation formed into a habit, then at the moment of death, relying only on the wish to achieve â€œten thoughts continuallyâ€ â€” how could one possibly do it?

[Consciousness more restless than apes] The six consciousnesses (eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness) are even more unsettled than a monkey that leaps and scrambles wildly. [Formed into a habit] Through repeated practice, making it become an instinct.

[Each should, with three or five companions of like mind, agree beforehand in words, that at the moment of death they will alternately awaken and instruct one another, reciting the name of Amitabha for the dying person and encouraging him to be reborn in the Land of Peace and Bliss, voice following voice, so as to accomplish the ten thoughts. It is like a wax seal stamped into clay: the seal is destroyed and the inscription is formed. When this life is cut off, that is the moment of rebirth in the Land of Peace and Bliss. Once one enters the class of the rightly fixed, what is there still to worry about? Each should weigh this great benefit â€” why not prepare the ten thoughts in advance?]

Therefore, it is best for everyone to invite three or five companions of like mind and agree beforehand: at the moment of death, they will alternately awaken and instruct, reciting the name of Amitabha Buddha for the dying one, encouraging him to firmly fix his vow of rebirth in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss, voice following voice, so as to accomplish the ten thoughts of continual recitation at death. It is like
a wax seal stamped into clay: though the seal is destroyed, the inscription is already formed;

so when the breath is cut off, that is the moment of rebirth in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss. Once one reaches the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss, at once he enters the class of the rightly fixed â€” and at that time, what is there still to worry about? Each of you must weigh this great benefit: why not prepare in advance the ten thoughts of continual recitation?
[In succession] following one after another. [A wax seal stamped into clay,
the seal
destroyed
and the inscription (
the pattern
) is formed] A wax seal carved with a pattern is pressed onto a clay mold. Heated and dried, when the wax melts, the pattern on the clay mold is formed. The clay mold is used to cast metal vessels.
The Nirvana Sutra says:
â€œLike a wax seal stamped into clay, the seal and the clay unite; the seal disappears and the inscription is formed.â€

Here â€œthe seal destroyed and the inscription formedâ€ is a metaphor for using our physical body to practice, accomplishing the ten thoughts of continual recitation at death; when the breathing stops, though the physical body dies (the seal is destroyed), the great matter of rebirth is at the same time accomplished (the inscription is formed) â€” â€œwhen this life is cut off, that is the moment of rebirth in the Land of Peace and Bliss.â€ [The class of the rightly fixed] One of the three classes. [Three classes] The three classes are three types of sentient beings. These three classes are: the class of the rightly fixed, the class of the wrongly fixed, and the class of the unfixed. The class of the rightly fixed refers to the type of sentient beings who will certainly realize enlightenment; the class of the wrongly fixed refers to the type who will ultimately never realize it; the class of the unfixed refers to the type who lies between right and wrong, possibly realizing and possibly not realizing. [Why not prepare the ten thoughts in advance?] Why not train in advance the ten thoughts of continual recitation? This is what Master Yongming, in the passage above, called â€œpreparing the ferry and the bridge.â€
Master Daochuo, in the Collected Essays on the Peaceful Grove, has two further very important instructions on rebirth through recitation:
[Even if one has committed evil throughout a whole life,
if only he can bind his mind in single-minded focus
, and constantly recitate the Buddhaâ€™s name, all obstructions will naturally be removed, and he will certainly attain rebirth.]
This passage says: even if one has committed evil throughout a whole life,
yet after repentance and turning,
if he can
bind his mind in single-minded focus
(pure thought following in succession), and often recitate the Buddhaâ€™s name, then all obstructions are naturally removed, and he will certainly attain rebirth.

Please note: â€œEven if one has committed evil throughout a whole lifeâ€ is the situation before repentance; â€œif only he can bind his mind in single-minded focus, and constantly recitate the Buddhaâ€™s nameâ€ is the situation after repentance. For if there is no sincere repentance, how could one accomplish binding his mind in single-minded focus?

[From the utmost of a whole life down to ten thoughts, all are reborn. The moment one reaches that land, he enters the class of the rightly fixed â€” equal in merit to practicing the Way for ten thousand kalpas!]

From the utmost of a whole life of thought-after-thought continuity, down to the ten thoughts of continual recitation at death, all are reborn in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss. The moment one reaches the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss, he enters the class of the rightly fixed â€” this is equal in merit to the effect of practicing the Way by the ordinary path for ten thousand kalpas!

[From the utmost of a whole life down to ten thoughts] Viewed from the whole of the Collected Essays on the Peaceful Grove, the meaning is: from the utmost of a whole life of thought-after-thought continuity, down to the ten thoughts of continual recitation at death. The ancients, in writing, prized concision, so when understanding it one must link the preceding and following passages together â€” never infer meaning from the words alone, nor take a passage out of context.
